newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Aide denies newspaper report on Yeltsin health.
newsitem.headline: Aide denies newspaper report on Yeltsin health.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary denied allegations published by a British newspaper on Monday that the Kremlin leader had a 50:50 chance of surviving a proposed heart operation and could work only 15 minutes a day.
Sergei Yastrzhembsky said in a statement that the article in the Financial Times, which he said had apparently pushed down Russian debt prices in London, was wrong from beginning to end.

"The London Financial Times today published an article about the state of health of the Russian president which... contains a completely false assertion that 'Yeltsin can work only 15 minutes a day'," the statement said. "The article also contains other assertions which have nothing to do with reality."

Yastrzhembsky said the report was "saturated with unconfirmed information quoting anonymous sources which apparently caused a considerable fall in Russia's foreign debt prices on the London securities market".

The Financial Times quoted unspecified Kremlin sources as saying Yeltsin had suffered a stroke as well as a heart attack between the two rounds of the presidential election in June and July and that since then he had been unable to sign documents.
The front-page report said his chief-of-staff, Anatoly Chubais, signed documents for the president using a rubber signature stamp.

Russian debt took a nosedive on international markets on Monday on fears about Yeltsin's health, reversing the euphoria of early last week set off by hopes that Russia would soon receive a good credit rating for its forthcoming first Eurobond.
Russian shares and bonds also fell.
Dealers said Western operators were selling the dollar-denominated MinFins, which are widely traded outside Russia, most actively, with local operators following the trend.
"Everything is going down on this news... Even investment funds, which are generally not nervous and which bought MinFins long ago, are selling," Imperial Bank dealer Alexei Denisov said.
Yeltsin, 65, announced earlier this month that he had agreed to undergo bypass surgery to improve blood supply to his heart which the doctors said was crucial to keep him fit for the job.
He said in a televised interview that the operation would probably take place in late September.
But later a surgeoun tipped to be chosen to carry out the operation said that it could be postponed or even cancelled judging by the patient's conditions.
The statements made by surgeon Renat Akchurin at the weekend sparked speculation that Yeltsin was too ill to be operated on. The Kremlin fiercely denied it.
Leading Russian and foreign doctors are due to meet on Wednesday to decide whether the operation is safe for Yeltsin and if so when to hold it.
